source: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lecture 1, ~43-51 min
keypoints: The tempting 2D algorithm - find a 1D peak on the middle column j = m/2, then a 1D peak on that row - is efficient (log n) but incorrect.
Being correct and inefficient is better than being incorrect and efficient.
Counterexample: the algorithm may return 14 (a 1D peak on its row) even though 14 is not a 2D peak, because a 2D peak may not exist on row i.
The correct recursive algorithm picks the middle column j = m/2 and finds the GLOBAL MAXIMUM on that column, at position (i, j).
It then compares (i, j) only with its left neighbor (i, j-1) and right neighbor (i, j+1).
If (i, j) is greater than or equal to both horizontal neighbors, then (i, j) is a 2D peak, because as the column maximum it already dominates the up and down neighbors.
Otherwise the algorithm recurses into the half (left or right columns) that contains the larger neighbor.
The problem set contains four different algorithms that students must analyze for complexity, efficiency, and correctness.
